title: Marathas and the Decline of the Mughals

cards.b: The Marathas, Sikhs and regional nawabs filled the space left by the Mughals. They matter to the story of how the British found it easy to expand.

Shivaji (1630 to 1680), son of Shahaji Bhonsle, took Torna (1646) and built Raigad. Killed Afzal Khan (1659). Attacked Surat (1664); Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Jai Singh; visited Aurangzeb at Agra (1666) and escaped. Coronation at Raigad (1674) as Chhatrapati. Southern campaign (Jinji, Vellore, 1677 to 78).

Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Pandit Rao, Nyayadhish. Revenue: ryotwari-like, with chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (extra one-tenth) from neighbouring territory. Salaried army, strong forts, navy (Kanhoji Angre later). Reduced the role of deshmukhs and abolished jagirs. Hill forts and guerrilla war (ganimi kava).

Sambhaji executed in 1689; Rajaram; Tarabai. Shahu was released in 1707; civil war with Tarabai; Treaty of Warna (1731) split Kolhapur and Satara. Peshwas from Balaji Vishwanath (1713 to 20) took control: Baji Rao I (1720 to 40), Balaji Baji Rao (1740 to 61). Maratha confederacy: Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Bhonsle (Nagpur), Gaekwad (Baroda). Raids reached Delhi, Orissa, the south.

At the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao. About 100,000 died. It broke Maratha reach and weakened the north. Mahadji Scindia revived their power; Nana Phadnavis in Pune. Three Anglo-Maratha wars: 1775 to 82 (Treaty of Salbai), 1803 to 05, 1817 to 18, ending Maratha power.

After Aurangzeb (1707) came weak rulers. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi (1739; took the Peacock Throne). Abdali’s raids. Successor states: Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh (Saadat Khan), Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk, 1724), Rohillas, Jats (Suraj Mal), Sikhs (Ranjit Singh later), Mysore (Haidar Ali), Travancore (Marthanda Varma). The Mughal emperor became a figurehead; Shah Alam II.

Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan (Adi Granth, 1604; killed 1606), Guru Hargobind, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Guru Gobind Singh (Khalsa, 1699; died 1708). Banda Bahadur’s rebellion (1709 to 1716). Misls in the 18th century; Ranjit Singh (1799 to 1839) unified the Punjab, the Sikh Empire. The Jats (Gokula, Raja Ram, Churaman, Suraj Mal at Bharatpur).

cards.h: Who is to blame for decline?
cards.b: Jadunath Sarkar blamed Aurangzeb; Marxist writers (Irfan Habib) blamed the jagirdari and agrarian crisis. Revisionists (Chetan Singh, Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly) see an 18th-century of regional growth and new prosperity, not a dark age. On the Marathas, Grant Duff praised Shivaji; Govind Sakharam Sardesai and Jadunath Sarkar both studied them. Was Shivaji a Hindu or a national king? Historians (Satish Chandra) say a regional ruler with secular practice, including Muslims in the army.

Shivaji is a regional and national icon; Maharashtra’s politics uses his memory (statue and memorial debates). The Khalsa and Gurdwara reform shape Sikh identity; Ranjit Singh’s legacy is a Punjab emblem. Federal power-sharing between the centre and regional power has roots in this age. Indian Navy’s new ensign (2022) draws on Shivaji’s seal.
